title: Web Agents with World Models: Learning and Leveraging Environment Dynamics in Web Navigation

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to establish whether current SOTA LLMs understand web environment dynamics (action-to-next-state association) and motivate the need for a world model due to irreversible mistakes in long-horizon tasks. Paper [9] explicitly explores the potential of LLMs to operate as world models, focusing on their ability to predict action applicability and resulting world states, which aligns with the purpose of assessing LLMs' understanding of web environment dynamics. Paper [7] also discusses the limitations of LLMs in global and local planning due to their poor understanding of the "real" physical world, motivating the need for a mental world knowledge model. Both papers share the same problem-class level objective of evaluating LLMs' understanding of environment dynamics and motivating world models.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses two analyses: (I) binary next-state prediction (golden vs lexically similar wrong next state) and (II) testing whether access to action candidates' outcomes improves optimal action selection. Paper [9] employs similar mechanisms to test LLMs' ability to predict action applicability and resulting world states, which is substantively equivalent to next-state prediction and outcome-based action selection. Paper [7] also evaluates LLMs' planning capabilities by analyzing their understanding of world dynamics, which overlaps with the mechanism of testing action-to-next-state associations.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring next-state prediction accuracy and testing whether awareness of outcomes improves action selection. Paper [9] uses a similar evaluation design to assess LLMs' ability to predict action applicability and resulting states, which matches the benchmark family and metric semantics of next-state prediction accuracy. Paper [7] evaluates LLMs' planning capabilities in terms of their understanding of world dynamics, which aligns with the validation framework of testing action selection improvements based on world knowledge. Both papers reuse the same evaluation design principles.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM web-navigation agents and world models. Paper [1] explicitly addresses LLMs adapted for web navigation tasks, focusing on their limitations in handling challenging scenarios. Paper [2] introduces WebVoyager, a multimodal web agent evaluated in web simulators, which falls within the same application area of LLM web-navigation agents. Paper [9] discusses world models for intelligent agents, which directly overlaps with the domain of world models for LLM web-navigation agents. All three papers address the same general application area.

**PURPOSE: Establish whether current SOTA LLMs understand web environment dynamics (action-to-next-state association), motivating the need for a world model, since LLMs make irreversible mistakes in long-horizon web tasks.**

Paper [9] "Making Large Language Models into World Models with Precondition and Effect Knowledge" directly explores whether LLMs can function as world models by predicting action effects and preconditions. However, its purpose is to *show LLMs can be induced* to perform world model functions, not to *diagnose their absence* as motivation for building one. Paper [7] "Agent Planning with World Knowledge Model" discusses LLMs' "poor understanding of the 'real' physical world" and hallucinating actions, which is thematically related but focuses on planning agents, not diagnosing web-environment dynamics understanding. No prior paper specifically establishes the empirical relationship "current SOTA LLMs lack web environment dynamics understanding (action→next-state)" as a motivating finding for web agents. The closest is [9], but its purpose is demonstrating capability, not diagnosing absence. This purpose appears uncovered.

**MECHANISM: Two preliminary analyses on 100 WebArena instances with human-annotated golden trajectories: (I) binary next-state prediction with lexically similar distractors (difflib similarity); (II) test whether access to action outcomes improves optimal action selection.**

Paper [9] tests LLMs on "predicting the resulting world state after an action" — this is structurally similar to Analysis I. However, the specific design (binary forced-choice between golden vs. lexically-similar-wrong next state using difflib, on WebArena with human-annotated trajectories) is more specific. Paper [12] "Language models are better than humans at next-token prediction" compares LLM vs. human performance on prediction tasks, which is a generic comparison design. The binary forced-choice next-state prediction primitive in [9] is substantively equivalent to Analysis I's mechanism. Analysis II (testing whether outcome awareness improves action selection) resembles the setup in [7] where world knowledge improves planning, but as an analysis protocol. The core primitive of Analysis I — binary prediction of next state with a distractor — is covered by [9]'s world-state prediction experiments.

**EVALUATION: LLMs average 54.75% next-state-prediction accuracy vs. 83% human; Claude-3.5-Sonnet ~52% (near random). Confirms world models absent in GPT-4o/Claude-3.5-Sonnet. Analysis II: outcome awareness helps action selection.**

The evaluation design uses WebArena as a benchmark family (covered by [1], [2], [19] which all use WebArena or similar web-agent benchmarks), LLM-vs-human comparison (covered by [12]), and accuracy metrics. Paper [19] "AgentBoard" uses multi-turn LLM agent evaluation with analytical breakdowns. Paper [9] uses accuracy metrics for world-state prediction. The evaluation design (accuracy on forced-choice prediction, LLM vs. human comparison) is covered by [9] and [12] at the design level.

**DOMAIN: LLM web-navigation agents / world models.**

Papers [1], [2], [3], [7], [19] all work in the domain of LLM web-navigation agents. Paper [9] works on LLMs as world models. This domain is clearly covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to build the first LLM-based web agent augmented with a world model that simulates action outcomes for better decision-making without policy training. Paper [1] discusses language-guided world models for AI control, but its focus is on enabling human communication with world models rather than augmenting LLM-based web agents for decision-making. Paper [3] introduces a world knowledge model for LLM agents to improve planning, but it emphasizes global prior knowledge and local planning rather than simulation-based decision-making. Paper [6] builds a model-based agent with a world model, but it focuses on code-based representations and task planning rather than web navigation. None of the prior papers explicitly address the purpose of augmenting LLM-based web agents with a world model for policy-training-free decision-making.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves a world-model-augmented (WMA) web agent that simulates action outcomes at inference using a world model trained to output free-form natural-language descriptions of important state differences between time steps, avoiding repeated elements and long HTML inputs. Paper [1] introduces language-guided world models but does not describe transition-focused observation abstraction or simulation of action outcomes for web navigation. Paper [3] uses a world knowledge model for planning but does not train the model to output abstracted state differences. Paper [6] builds a world model but focuses on code-based representations rather than free-form natural-language descriptions. Paper [24] discusses state abstraction in reinforcement learning but does not apply it to web navigation or use natural-language descriptions. None of the prior papers describe the specific mechanism of transition-focused observation abstraction for web agents.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses WebArena, Mind2Web, and multimodal extensions to validate the WMA agent's performance. Paper [23] introduces WebArena as a realistic web environment for testing autonomous agents, and Paper [20] introduces Mind2Web as a dataset for evaluating generalist web agents. Both benchmarks are reused in this contribution, making the evaluation design covered. Additionally, the use of standard success rate (SR) metrics and cross-environment generalization aligns with existing evaluation designs in Papers [23] and [20].

### Domain
The domain is LLM web-navigation agents. Papers [4], [7], [8], [20], and [23] all work in the application area of LLM-based web agents for navigation and task completion. While this contribution targets specific benchmarks and tasks, the general application area of LLM web-navigation agents is well-covered by prior work.

**PURPOSE: Build the first LLM-based web agent augmented with a world model that simulates action outcomes for better (policy-training-free) decision-making.**

The purpose is to improve web agent decision-making at inference time by using a world model to simulate outcomes, without retraining the policy. Paper [3] ("Agent Planning with World Knowledge Model") explicitly aims to use world knowledge models to improve LLM agent planning by providing prior knowledge and reducing hallucinations — same objective of augmenting LLM agents with world models for better decision-making. Paper [1] ("Language-guided World Models") develops world models for AI agents to improve decision-making. However, neither [1] nor [3] specifically targets the "policy-training-free inference-time lookahead" framing for web agents. Paper [3] is closest: it uses a world knowledge model to guide LLM agent planning without retraining the policy model, targeting interactive planning tasks. The objective — augment an LLM agent with a world model to improve planning without policy retraining — is substantively equivalent at the problem-class level.

**MECHANISM: World model simulates next observation per action candidate; value function scores simulated observations; highest-reward action selected. Key novelty: transition-focused observation abstraction (free-form NL descriptions of only state differences).**

The core inference-time lookahead loop (simulate → score → select) appears in model-based RL literature (e.g., [13] PlaNet: "chooses actions through fast planning in the learned latent space"). Paper [6] (WorldCoder) builds a world model and uses it for planning. Paper [3] uses a world knowledge model to predict outcomes and guide action selection. However, the specific primitive of "transition-focused observation abstraction" — outputting only the important state *differences* in free-form natural language rather than full next-state representations — is not described in any prior paper. Papers [13], [14], [19] use latent-space abstractions in RL, not NL difference descriptions. Paper [3] uses world knowledge but doesn't describe transition-focused differential observation abstraction. No prior paper combines: (a) LLM-based world model generating NL state-difference descriptions, (b) a fine-tuned value function scoring those simulated observations, (c) inference-time best-action selection for web navigation. The transition-focused abstraction primitive is genuinely absent.

Paper [2] (AWM) evaluates on both WebArena and Mind2Web with success rate metrics and compares against baselines including MindAct — the same evaluation design (same benchmark families, same metric semantics, same comparison structure). The evaluation design (WebArena SR + Mind2Web cross-environment generalization, comparing against AWM/MindAct) is substantively covered by [2] and [23].

---

**DOMAIN: LLM web-navigation agents.**

Papers [2], [4], [7], [8], [20], [21], [22], [23] all work in the domain of LLM-based web navigation agents. This is clearly covered.

### Purpose
The contribution aims to demonstrate that a world-model agent is significantly more cost- and time-efficient than trial-and-error tree-search agents that execute actions in the environment. Paper [2] ("Tree Search for Language Model Agents") shares the same purpose at the problem-class level: it addresses the inefficiency of tree-search agents in decision-making tasks, specifically their struggle with multi-step reasoning and environmental feedback. Paper [6] ("WorldCoder, a Model-Based LLM Agent") also aligns with this purpose, as it emphasizes the sample and compute efficiency of model-based agents compared to trial-and-error approaches like deep RL. Paper [11] ("Agent Planning with World Knowledge Model") further supports this purpose by critiquing trial-and-error planning and proposing world-model-based agents for more efficient global planning. All three papers share the same objective of improving efficiency in agent inference by moving away from trial-and-error methods.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses a head-to-head comparison against a tree-search agent (Koh et al., 2024) on WebArena, measuring success rate (SR), API cost, and inference time per instruction. Paper [2] ("Tree Search for Language Model Agents") describes an inference-time search algorithm for LM agents, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism of comparing tree-search agents against other approaches. Paper [8] ("Multiagent Monte Carlo Tree Search") and Paper [9] ("Trial-Based Heuristic Tree-search for Distributed Multi-Agent Planning") also describe mechanisms involving direct comparisons of tree-search agents, albeit in different domains. These mechanisms are equivalent at the primitive level: evaluating tree-search agents against alternatives using performance metrics.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring success rate, API cost, and inference time per instruction, which are standard metrics for assessing agent efficiency. Paper [2] ("Tree Search for Language Model Agents") uses similar metrics to evaluate tree-search agents, including success rate and computational cost. Paper [6] ("WorldCoder, a Model-Based LLM Agent") also evaluates efficiency using metrics like sample efficiency and compute cost. Paper [14] ("Energy Efficiency Considerations for Popular AI Benchmarks") discusses energy efficiency trade-offs, which align with the evaluation design of measuring resource usage. These prior papers share the same evaluation design, even if applied to different benchmarks or datasets.

### Domain
The domain of the contribution is efficient LLM agent inference. Paper [2] ("Tree Search for Language Model Agents") operates in the same domain, focusing on autonomous agents powered by LLMs for decision-making tasks. Paper [6] ("WorldCoder, a Model-Based LLM Agent") also works in the domain of LLM-based agents, emphasizing their efficiency in task planning. Paper [11] ("Agent Planning with World Knowledge Model") further addresses LLM-based agent planning, critiquing trial-and-error methods and proposing world-model-based approaches. All three papers operate in the same general application area of efficient LLM agent inference.

The purpose is to demonstrate that a world-model-based LLM agent is more computationally efficient (cost and time) than tree-search agents on web tasks. Paper [6] (WorldCoder) mentions being "more compute-efficient compared to ReAct" for a world-model agent, which is close but focuses on gridworlds/task planning, not web agents. Paper [2] (Tree Search for Language Model Agents) introduces the tree search agent but does not compare efficiency against a world-model alternative — it's the baseline being compared against. **EVALUATION: WMA takes 140.3 sec/instance and $0.4 API cost vs Tree search agent's 748.3 sec and $2.7 (5.3x faster, 6.8x cheaper).**
